summary: Two Coast Guard range towers on the Delaware River at New Castle, Delaware: wooden lights first shown in 1876 to keep ships off Bulkhead Shoal; the steel towers that replaced them are closed to visitors.

light.characteristic: fixed white, 2 s on and 1 s eclipse (front light, from 31 Oct 1894; Light-House Board report 1895)
light.lamp: Funck lamp with silvered reflector (1876, LighthouseFriends)
light.illuminant_history: oil; incandescent oil vapor (rear 1914, front 1917); electric (front 1923, rear 1925)

structures.type: square wooden tower attached to the dwelling, detached and moved 30 ft west in 1886
structures.note: The 1878 description quoted by LighthouseFriends gives a 38 ft (11.6 m) tower; the USLHS record gives 15 ft (4.6 m). See notes_for_editor.
Light shows 56 ft (17 m) above mean high water (LighthouseFriends).

structures.type: square tower attached to its own dwelling

facts.agency: United States Coast Guard (the lights and towers); private owners (the front dwelling and land)

events.note: Both lights first exhibited on 15 November 1876
Front tower detached from the dwelling and moved 30 ft west; enclosed passage built; frame oil house erected
Front light changed on 31 October 1894 from fixed white to fixed white with 2 s on and 1 s eclipse
Sea wall rebuilt and jetties thrown out to protect it (fiscal year ended 30 June 1894)
Storms tore down about 90 ft of jetties at the front station, rebuilt (fiscal year ended 30 June 1896)

Steamship Ontario ran ashore off the station in the small hours of 15 Feb 1877; ice boats failed to move her on 17 Feb; lightened and towed up the river on 19 Feb; passed down outward bound on 20 Feb (keeper's log as printed by LighthouseFriends)
Lights temporarily discontinued 3 May to 26 July 1898; LighthouseFriends suggests a Spanish-American War precaution
Front tower repainted solid white; barn, dwelling and walk repainted light brown
Rear light: oil changed to incandescent oil vapor
Front light: oil changed to incandescent oil vapor
Wartime regulation of river traffic; patrol boats to be stationed at the intersections of the New Castle range with the Finns Point and Deep Water Point ranges (Evening Journal, 9 Apr 1917)
Front light electrified: small generator and storage battery in the tower; locomotive headlight marks the range; lens lantern shows sectors
Rear light: incandescent oil vapor changed to electric incandescent

Bulletin notes a fire at the rear dwelling from a paint burner some years earlier: smoke about two hours after work ended, fire in sheathing and studding; serious fire avoided with difficulty. Fire undated; year is the bulletin's year
Front property put up for auction by the Coast Guard; high bidders paid $5,000 (LighthouseFriends)
Front tower demolished and replaced by a modern steel skeletal tower; keepers' house survives (USLHS place record). LighthouseFriends dates the replacement to the 1960s
Rear light discontinued, per the USLHS rear record (Year Discontinued: 1964). LighthouseFriends gives no date for the rear's automated beacon
Rear tower and dwelling burned to the ground in November 1982, on the owner's hire of the Goodwill Fire Company (LighthouseFriends)

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends says the rear light's combined tower and dwelling was burned to the ground in November 1982 by the Goodwill Fire Company. The USLHS rear record also still reads existing, which the sources read do not support.

LighthouseFriends gives the front light at 39.642391, -75.595424 and the rear at 39.648162, -75.599037. The current point lies about 0.55 km from the front light and about 1.0 km from the rear. The proposed value is the midpoint of the pair. Review before applying.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The original wooden towers were replaced piecemeal. The front tower was replaced by a steel tower in 1964 (USLHS place record; LighthouseFriends says the 1960s). The USLHS rear record gives 1964 as the year the rear light was discontinued, but its own record still reads Existing: Yes, and LighthouseFriends gives no date for the rear's automated beacon. The rear date is reported as the archive's, not settled. The steel tower still shows a light.

notes_for_editor: (1) Keepers at the front light, 1930s: USLHS roster lists Milton A. Duffield as head keeper 1933-1943; LighthouseFriends calls Arthur W. Hopkins the last keeper and says he stayed as custodian until at least 1940. Both sources name Duffield (1933-1943); they disagree on who was the last keeper. Both kept in the story; not reconciled. (2) Davis, 1948: USLHS gives Arthur W. Davis; LighthouseFriends gives William A. Davis. (3) Front tower height: the 1878 description quoted by LighthouseFriends gives 38 ft (11.6 m); the USLHS record gives tower 15 ft (4.6 m) and focal height 20 ft. The record's 4.6 m is kept; not corrected. (4) Rear tower: LighthouseFriends quotes 50 ft (15 m) from base to focal plane; USLHS rear record gives tower 50 ft and focal height 90 ft (27 m). The record's 27.0 m for the rear is the USLHS focal height. The rear's original house-tower is burned, so the 27.0 m entry should be read as historic. (5) The rear's replacement tower: no date in the sources read; the record gives 1953 and 1964 for different towers. Not used. (6) The front's steel tower: USLHS says 1964; LighthouseFriends says 1960s. Story uses 1964 from the USLHS record and says 1960s from LighthouseFriends. (7) Checked on the page images: item 495, New Castle range (front), is the heading on printed p. 87 (scan 102); its sod sentence (800 sq ft) and 96 trees run onto printed p. 88 (scan 103), where item 496, New Castle range (rear), has about 76 trees. The 800 sq ft and 96 trees belong to the front station. Footnote cites scan 102-103, not scan 104. (8) The 1901 repainting entry (p. scan 138) has an OCR item number that reads '50o' and is matched to New Castle range front by name. (9) The USCG Historian's archived copy (web.archive.org captures) returned 403 or an empty capture and was not read. The Coast Guard's own dates are not checked. (10) The 1917 newspaper page is OCR. The passage on patrol boats was read from OCR text (LOC page). Two OCR passages of the same page agree on the two intersections; the page image was not viewed. (11) The 1929 bulletin fire is undated ('some years ago'). The story does not date it. The 1924-1929 Bulletin index also lists 'New Castle Range Rear light station ignited by paint burner' at page 66; that entry was not read and is not cited. (12) The Wikipedia leads (a 1975 fire at the rear house; 1953 and 1964 tower dates; the rear light characteristic 'continuous green light') were not cited. (13) No women keepers or family members of the keepers are named in the sources read; the roster lists men only. (14) LighthouseFriends is copyrighted: the story paraphrases it, with only short quotations in the evidence. (15) The front dwelling is a private residence. The buyers of 1953 and their descendants are not named. (16) The position correction (location) is a proposal for a human to check. (17) The sod and tree figures and the 1894 jetty entry carry no storm cause in the sources. The story does not say a storm caused them except for the 1896 entry, which says storms.
